Chapter Ten: The Irreversibility of Existence
There’s something almost invisible about the finality of being born. It’s so easy to overlook, isn’t it? Once someone comes into existence, there’s simply no way to undo that fact. All the risks, the hurts, and the challenges of life—they’re no longer out there as possibilities. They become real, and that person has to find their own way through them.
Imagine a teenager, wrestling with anxiety and all the uncertainty that comes with growing up. Maybe, in their lowest moments, they wish they could go back and choose not to exist at all. But that choice? It’s not theirs. Once existence has begun, it can’t be reversed.
This idea—the irreversibility of existence—is at the heart of a huge moral question. Deciding to bring someone into the world isn’t just a temporary thing. It’s permanent. No matter how much pain or suffering a person might face, that decision can't be taken back. And those risks? They’re not just some far-off worry—they become someone’s lived reality.
For people who are already here, life is about making the most of what we have, searching for meaning, and finding moments of happiness. But for someone who doesn’t exist yet, there’s a deeper question: Is it right to put someone into an irreversible situation—one they never consented to in the first place?
Our teenager might find ways to cope. Maybe they lean on friends, or find comfort in family. They learn to face their struggles, even if they never chose to be alive in the first place. But the truth remains: those harms can’t be erased. The fact of existence is permanent.
Suddenly, the whole question of procreation feels heavier, doesn’t it? It’s not only about hope or love—it’s a decision that shapes someone’s entire life, for better or for worse. The unchangeable nature of being born forces us to look at the risks and harms of life in a whole new way.
